podcasts.name: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comparison to Classical Music Dislike
podcast.body: Mozart is used as an example in an analogy to explain the "lack of knowledge" argument against trap music. Dismissing all trap music because of a few artists is compared to disliking classical music and thus rejecting Mozart, highlighting a superficial understanding. "eso es como si digo no me gusta mozar no me gusta bángler no me gusta la música clásica y el tercero que es más vergonzoso es lo que se llama la falacia narcisista."

srcs.episode: EL TRAP SÍ ES MÚSICA. (Aunque a lo mejor no te guste)

podcast.title: Creative Process Comparison
podcast.body: Ash's evolved creative process, characterized by direct "downloads" of musical information, was compared to Mozart's work as described by Salieri in the movie "Amadeus." Salieri noted Mozart's scores had "no eraser marks" or "corrections," suggesting a genius that takes "dictation." "Solary says, when he was looking at Mozart's work, he said, there's no eraser marks. There's no corrections. It's almost like he's taking dictation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: USS In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Cultural Significance of Scatology
podcast.body: Mozart's use of scatological humor in his compositions and letters provides insight into his sense of humor and that of his contemporaries, reinforcing the idea that such humor was more mainstream in 18th-century polite society and contributing to the field of scatter linguistics. "it reinforces the thinking that scatter logical humor was way more mainstream back then, including in polite society than it is today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Defiance of Conventions
podcast.body: Mozart frequently defied the conventions of his era, often making fun of the nobility in his letters and refusing to conform to the seriousness of the world that celebrated him. He inverted hierarchies in his operas and ridiculed societal solidity from within, living a fast and dying young, leaving behind a legacy of chaos and contradiction. "Mozart no quería volver ningún sistema, pero se reía de todos."

srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Medical Benefits of Listening to Music
podcast.body: Research suggests that listening to Mozart's music can enhance the effectiveness of ibuprofen. When paired with the medication, it can also reduce inflammation by up to 93%. "listening to Mozart increases the effectiveness of ibuprofen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind Blowing Facts in 60 Minutes: The 5th Edition

podcast.title: Obscene Personal Letters
podcast.body: Mozart also wrote obscene letters for fun to various family members, including his father, mother, wife, sister, cousin, and several friends. "Mozart also wrote obscene letters for fun to his father, his mother, his wife, his sister, his cousin, and a bunch of friends."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pain Management Study with Ibuprofen
podcast.body: Researchers at the University of Utah conducted a study revealing that listening to Mozart while taking ibuprofen significantly enhances pain relief. While ibuprofen alone reduced inflammation by 70%, the combination with Mozart music further decreased inflammation from 70% to 90%, suggesting a notably greater reduction in pain. Though currently tested on mice, these findings could lead to new human pain management methods if replicated in human trials. "when they gave pain sufferers ibuprofen and had them listen to Mozart at the same time, that inflammation decreased when from 70% to 90%."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Mind-blowing Facts about Music, the Brain, and the Body

podcast.title: Performance Analogy by MF Doom
podcast.body: MF Doom used the example of attending "The Marriage of Figaro" without expecting to see Mozart himself to illustrate his philosophy that the art itself, not the physical presence of the artist, is the essence of a performance. "De hecho tu por ejemplo cuando vas a ver las bodas de fígado evidentemente no esperas verte a Mozart y puede ir a disfrutar las bodas de fígado y tampoco es el único que ha ido en este camino."

srcs.episode: MF DOOM. Repaso de un genio

podcast.title: Prolific Classical Composer
podcast.body: Mozart is widely considered the greatest composer of all time, having written more than 800 works that touched on all Western classical genres within his 35 years of life. "In his 35 years, Mozart wrote more than 800 works that touched on all the western classical genres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sanitized Lyrics Posthumously
podcast.body: After Mozart's death, his widow sought to publish his more risqué works like "Lechmik Im Arch," but due to their explicit nature, the lyrics were sanitized for almost 200 years, with the original versions only being widely made public in 1991. "But since they were so gross, the lyrics were sanitized for almost 200 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scatological Humor in Compositions
podcast.body: Mozart had a penchant for writing songs about "poop and weird sex," evident in a sizable collection of canons, including the famous "Lechmik Im Arch" (Kiss My Ass). "Mozart was also gross. He also loved to write songs about hoop and weird sex."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scatological Letters and Lyrics
podcast.body: Approximately 12% of Mozart's letters to his friends and associates contained at least one reference to poop. Some of his song lyrics also included scatological content, necessitating changes by other individuals. This aspect of his personality is so notable that it has been speculated to be linked to a case of Tourette's. "Approximately 12% of all Mozart's letters to friends and associates had at least one reference to poop in it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Mozart Effect – Enhanced Intellect Theory
podcast.body: The "Mozart effect" is a theory suggesting that exposing fetuses and babies to classical music can enhance a child's intellect in the womb, potentially leading to better math skills, spatial perception, and 8-9 IQ points higher. Studies at various universities appeared to confirm this, leading to the state of Georgia allocating $100,000 annually to provide every newborn with a classical music CD or tape. However, later research, including a 1999 project, questioned the theory, finding that babies received similar benefits from listening to Mozart as from listening to a parent read a Stephen King novel.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
